summary.text: Damping is the loss of energy from an oscillating system, which reduces or prevents its oscillation.
Sources include fluid drag, surface friction, radiation and electrical resistance, and the amount of damping decides how the system behaves.
A damping ratio describes how damped a system is: low values overshoot and ring, one value just avoids overshoot, and higher values creep back slowly.

facts.label: Damping ratio symbol
facts.value: Written as zeta, a number with no units

facts.label: Critical damping
facts.value: Returns to equilibrium in the least time

facts.label: Undamped case
facts.value: The mass would bounce forever at equal height

facts.label: Q factor
facts.value: A high Q means slow damping relative to the oscillation

items.prompt: You drop a weight on a spring into a tub of thick syrup and it oozes back to rest without ever passing the middle. What kind of damping is this?

options.label: Overdamped
Underdamped
Undamped
Critically damped

items.explain: High losses, such as a viscous fluid, let the mass return slowly without overshooting, which is called overdamped.

items.prompt: A bounce on a pogo-like spring gets a little lower each time, and keeps crossing the middle. What does that tell you?

options.label: It is overdamped and stuck in place
It is critically damped
It has no damping at all here
It is underdamped, shedding energy

items.explain: Underdamped systems overshoot repeatedly, dissipating some energy each time, so the oscillations die toward zero.

items.prompt: A hotel wants a door that swings shut as fast as it can without slamming back open. Which damping level suits it?

options.label: Underdamped, so it bounces shut
Critically damped, the edge of no overshoot
Overdamped, so it creeps closed
Undamped, so it never slows

items.explain: Critical damping is the level at which the system just fails to overshoot, and it returns to equilibrium in the minimum amount of time.

items.prompt: Friction on a sliding crate and damping of a bouncing spring are often mixed up. What is the correct relationship?

options.label: They are the same thing under two names
Damping is a force, friction is an energy
Friction can cause damping, but the two are not identical
Friction prevents damping from occurring

items.explain: Friction is a dissipative force acting on a system and can cause or contribute to damping, but damping is not to be confused with it.

items.prompt: An engineer says a system's damping ratio is 0.4. Compared with a ratio of 1, how will it behave?

options.label: It overshoots and oscillates before settling
It returns slowly without any overshoot
It never moves from equilibrium
It oscillates forever at one size

items.explain: A ratio between 0 and 1 is underdamped, which means overshooting with decaying oscillation; 1 is the critical case.

items.prompt: A glass bell keeps ringing for a very long time compared with the length of one vibration before it fades. How does its Q factor read?

options.label: Small, since it loses energy quickly
Large, since the damping is slow
Zero, since it is perfectly steady
Unrelated, since Q ignores damping

items.explain: Q is a non-dimensional measure of the amount of damping, and a high Q indicates slow damping relative to the oscillation.

paragraphs.heading: What damping is
paragraphs.text: Damping is anything inside or acting on a vibrating system that shrinks its swings or stops them happening at all. In physical systems, it is the loss of energy from the motion, a process called dissipation. Damping should not be confused with friction. Friction is one kind of force that drains energy, and it can cause damping or add to it.

paragraphs.heading: Where it comes from
paragraphs.text: Damping turns up in many forms. A fluid can drag on a moving object, surfaces can rub, a system can radiate energy away, electrical resistance can sap an electronic oscillator, and light can be absorbed or scattered inside optical ones. Some systems, such as those found in living things and in bikes, also show damping that does not rest on losing energy.

paragraphs.heading: A weight on a spring
paragraphs.text: Many systems start to oscillate when they are nudged away from a resting balance point, called equilibrium. A weight hung from a spring is the classic case: pull it down, let go, and it bobs up and down. Each bounce carries it back toward equilibrium, but it shoots past. Losses such as friction can make these swings fade gradually toward nothing.

paragraphs.heading: Undamped, underdamped, overdamped
paragraphs.text: How much damping a system has decides how it moves. With no losses at all, the weight would keep bouncing forever, each bounce as high as the last; this imagined case is called undamped. Usually the weight overshoots again and again, losing a little energy every time, until the swings die out; this is called underdamped. With heavy losses, as when the experiment is done in a thick, syrupy fluid, the weight creeps back to rest without ever overshooting; this is called overdamped.

paragraphs.heading: Critical damping
paragraphs.text: Between underdamped and overdamped lies one particular amount of damping at which the system only just fails to overshoot and makes not a single swing. This is called critical damping. What sets it apart from overdamping is speed: a critically damped system gets back to equilibrium in the least possible time.

paragraphs.heading: The damping ratio
paragraphs.text: A single number called the damping ratio, written ζ (zeta), sums up how damped a system is. It has no units, because it is a ratio of two coefficients measured in the same units. A value of ζ = 0 means undamped, values between 0 and 1 mean underdamped, ζ = 1 is critically damped, and anything above 1 is overdamped. The larger the ratio, the more damped the system.

paragraphs.heading: The fading wave
paragraphs.text: An underdamped system traces a damped sine wave: a smooth wave whose height shrinks toward zero as time goes on. Such waves appear all over science and engineering, wherever an oscillator loses energy faster than it is being fed. Another unit-free measure, the Q factor, equals 1 / (2 ζ). A high Q means the swings die away slowly compared with how fast they repeat.

paragraphs.heading: Why engineers care
paragraphs.text: Oscillating behaviour matters in control, chemical, mechanical, structural and electrical engineering. What oscillates varies widely, from a tall building swaying in the wind to the speed of an electric motor. Describing the motion with unit-free numbers, like the damping ratio, makes it easier to see what all these cases have in common.
